newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS-MOL global IPO seen fully subscribed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-MOL global IPO seen fully subscribed.

text.p: A forthcoming global offering of shares in the Hungarian oil and gas company MOL, involving an at least 12.5 percent stake, is likely to be fully subscribed, analysts said on Thursday.

The state privatisation agency announced Wednesday evening that it would offer 12.5 percent in MOL to international investors, while the global co-ordinators will have an over-allotment option on a further 2.5 percent stake.
An international roadshow between April 21 and May 2, and the pricing and allocation on May 6, will be followed by a domestic offering of either one or two percent of MOL shares.
Analysts said both the global and the international offering was likely to attract sufficient demand.
"(The amount offered) is realistic, not too large and it will be sold," said Andrea Dicso of Bank Austria Investment Rt, adding that the market expected oversubscription on the domestic offering.
Analysts said the price of the shares was likely to be set at levels close to 3,000 forints, compared with MOL's closing price at 3,135 forints on the Budapest Stock Exchange (BSE) on Thursday.
They agreed that market rumours that the price may be as low as 2,850 forints, were not justified.
Analysts said the interest in MOL's shares was reinforced by the company raising its net income to 22.2 billion forints last year from 1.1 billion in 1995 and carrying out a cost cutting programme.

They added that the recent deregulation of Hungary's energy prices, a substantial improvement in the Hungarian economy and MOL's expansion in the countries around Hungary also made MOL A London analyst, who declined to be named, said investors would probably be wrong to question the government's intention to allow the market to decide energy prices or to doubt MOL management's determination to see through serious cost cutting.

"Cost cutting has already shown results expressed in figures," the analyst said. "And the government has been sending positive signals recently and it knows that it will have to return to the share market within 12 months."
Hungary plans to privatise a further substantial stake in MOL within a year.
Roger Monson, London-based chief equity strategist at Daiwa Europe Ltd said MOL's position on an increasingly competitive domestic market was firm.
"They will lose some (market share) but probably not a large amount."
Some analysts said economic developments in the U.S. are likely to influence the demand for MOL shares.
"On an IPO of this magnitude...the situation of the U.S. market has a strong influence." said Spencer Jakab of CSFB's Budapest unit.
He said the flow of money into U.S. funds has slowed down recently due to interest rate hike expectations.
Analysts said a rise in U.S. interest rates would probably weaken demand for MOL shares although the effect was unlikely to be very strong.
"The market sentiment abroad is not perfect, but (MOL) is a good paper and everybody sees that (buying MOL shares) is good business," Dicso said.

She said that foreign investors expecting a price discount at the global offering were currently sellers of MOL shares on the BSE but demand from domestic investors, which has strengthened substantially since early 1996 on strong gains on the BSE, were still pushing MOL's price upward.
Analysts added that Spain's and Poland's plans about the privatisation of their oil companies this year were not likely to influence the MOL IPO substantially.
